response.passage: Microorganisms, or germs, are invisible to the naked eye and exist everywhere, even on surfaces that appear perfectly clean. Because they are microscopic, you cannot rely on your eyes to judge if your hands are safe; they may harbor pathogens even when they look spotless. Effective handwashing is the most critical defense against these invisible threats. Simply rinsing with water is insufficient because germs are often protected by natural oils on our skin that water alone cannot remove. Using plain soap for at least twenty seconds is essential, as soap molecules physically break down the oily layer and lift germs away, regardless of whether the soap is labeled antibacterial. Furthermore, germs do not only spread through direct contact with sick individuals; they travel through contaminated surfaces and respiratory droplets. When you cough or sneeze, you must cover your mouth with a tissue or your elbow rather than your bare palm, as palms easily transfer pathogens to everything you touch. Finally, remember that antibiotics are specialized medicines designed only to fight bacterial infections. They are completely ineffective against viruses like the common cold or flu. Taking them unnecessarily or stopping a prescribed course early contributes to antibiotic resistance, making future infections harder to treat. Always complete the full course of medicine as directed by your doctor to ensure the infection is fully eliminated.
response.summary: Germs are invisible pathogens that require proper handwashing with soap rather than just water to be removed effectively. It is important to practice good respiratory hygiene and use antibiotics only for bacterial infections as prescribed.
